title: Observational evidence for cloud cover enhancement over western European forests

settings.description: Ten years (2004-2013) of 15-minute Meteosat Second Generation SEVIRI imagery over western European temperate forests without pronounced orography, evaluated for daylight hours 6-18 UTC.
The Landes region, a planted maritime pine forest larger than 12,000 km2, JJA temperature 20.9 C and JJA precipitation 143 mm.
The Sologne region, dominated by original broadleaf oak cover, JJA temperature 19.3 C and JJA precipitation 150 mm.
Cloud frequency derived with the physics-based MSG-CPP algorithm using multiple low-resolution channels and a cloud optical thickness threshold of 0.3.
Cloud frequency derived independently with the empirical MSG-HRV algorithm using only the 1 km high-resolution visible broadband channel.
The June-August summer stratum used for the main cloud frequency contrast.
The remainder of the year, analysed for Sologne to establish the seasonal switch in cloud preference.
Diurnal stratification of JJA cloud cover into the early morning development phase, the 11-13 UTC window, and the 15-16 UTC evening persistence phase.
Landes days classified by 10 m meridional wind speed and direction, contrasting calm conditions with regional average wind speeds above 1 m/s.
The same wind classification applied to the smaller Sologne forest, where edge effects are harder to detect.
Days stratified by sea level pressure to test dependence on synoptic conditions.
The 2004-2008 period over the Landes area that later suffered maximum windthrow, used as the reference for the cyclone Klaus natural experiment.
The 2009-2013 period following the 24 January 2009 landfall of cyclone Klaus and the resulting windthrow of the Landes forest.
Boxes outside the storm-affected area and the Sologne region, used as controls for the Klaus analysis.

claims.from: forest versus surrounding agricultural land cover
claims.statement: For both regions summertime clouds occur more frequently over forest than over surrounding agricultural land, with a fractional JJA cloud frequency increase generally in the range 0.05-0.15.
The spatial pattern of cloud frequency closely resembles the pattern of forest cover.
The MSG-CPP and MSG-HRV products yield similar spatial patterns, so the contrast is not an artefact of one retrieval.
Sensitivity analyses show the result is robust over a range of cloud detection thresholds.

claims.to: significance of the cloud frequency contrast
claims.statement: Daily JJA forest minus non-forest cloud frequency differences are significant for both regions but markedly stronger for Landes than for Sologne.
claims.match_note: Not extracted, so forest size as a modulating condition is missing from the graph.

claims.statement: Non-forested boxes do not differ significantly from each other, showing that the forest-induced change is independent of regional-scale gradients in cloud climatology.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. This is the paper's own control result.

claims.to: cloud occurrence confined to forest and occasional deep convection
claims.statement: High-resolution snapshots reveal conditions in which clouds occur only over forest, and in isolated cases this develops into preferred triggering of deep convection.

claims.to: significance of the forest cloud preference
claims.statement: For Sologne there is a significant preference for clouds over forest during JJA, while outside that period the difference in cloud frequency is not significant.
Over forest clouds develop earlier and faster, peaking around 08:00 UTC, and persist longer into the evening with a peak difference at 15:00-16:00 UTC.

claims.to: forest minus non-forest cloud frequency difference
claims.statement: There is no significant forest minus non-forest difference between 11 and 13 UTC, probably because clouds have developed fully over both surfaces.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. A time-of-day null result that the counting rules require to be kept.

claims.to: cloud frequency at the downwind forest edge
claims.statement: Landes shows consistently higher cloud frequency at the downwind and to a lesser extent the cross-wind forest edge under all wind directions, most pronounced above about 1 m/s regional average wind speed.

claims.from: regional wind conditions at the smaller Sologne forest
claims.statement: No clear relation between cloud frequency patterns and regional wind conditions was found for the smaller Sologne forest, where edge effects are harder to detect.

claims.from: synoptic conditions measured by sea level pressure
claims.to: forest minus non-forest cloud frequency difference
claims.statement: No strong dependence was found between sea level pressure and the cloud frequency difference, suggesting the contrast occurs under a range of synoptic conditions with possibly different dominant mechanisms.
claims.match_note: Not extracted; distinct from the wind-speed result already captured by CL008.

claims.to: land surface temperature contrast between forest and surroundings
claims.statement: Land surface temperature rises progressively over surrounding areas through summer, by up to 10 K for Sologne, while forest LST stays stable, indicating sustained forest evapotranspiration against declining evaporation outside.

claims.from: sudden forest removal by cyclone Klaus windthrow
claims.statement: Over the most damaged Landes area, JJA cloud frequency fell by up to 0.20 in 2009-2013 relative to 2004-2008.

claims.from: areas outside the storm damage and the Sologne region
claims.statement: No significant cloud frequency change was found for boxes outside the storm-affected area or for Sologne, isolating the windthrow effect.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. This control is what makes the Klaus result attributable.

claims.from: sudden forest removal by cyclone Klaus windthrow
claims.to: seasonal amplitude of the forest minus non-forest cloud difference
claims.statement: The seasonal amplitude of the forest minus non-forest cloud difference fell from 0.114 before 2009 to 0.020 afterwards, almost an order of magnitude.

claims.to: recovery of the forest cloud effect
claims.statement: The recovery time of these forests with respect to their impact on cloud formation is well over five years and possibly much longer.
Albedo is 0.11-0.14 over the Sologne and Landes forests against 0.16-0.19 over the more reflective surroundings, a difference large enough to affect boundary-layer growth.
claims.match_note: Not extracted as its own record, although it is the quantitative basis of the proposed mechanism.

claims.statement: In Sologne the enhanced vegetation index starts higher outside the forest but falls strongly through summer because of harvesting, producing strong surface warming of the surroundings.
At Landes the spatial vegetation index contrast is small and of variable sign in late summer, so canopy structure alone is not a main determinant of the cloud frequency difference.

claims.from: forest surface properties, lower albedo and higher roughness
claims.to: boundary layer thermal convection and moistening
claims.statement: The authors' conceptual model attributes the cloud enhancement to lower albedo and higher roughness producing larger turbulent exchange and thermal convection, amplified by frictional convergence and a forest breeze.
The broadleaf-dominated Sologne forest shows increased cloud occurrence relative to its surroundings.
claims.match_note: Same direction and endpoints, scoped to the broadleaf region.

claims.statement: The broadleaf Sologne forest shows earlier cloud onset and longer persistence than its surroundings.
claims.match_note: Same direction and endpoints, scoped to the broadleaf region.
